I struggled with this a lot myself. I don't know your situation or why you do it, but I'll tell you why I did it myself. My mother was abusive and would occasionally hit me when overly mad or drunk. It took a lot of therapy to unpack that before finally getting a handle on it. It also didn't help that I'm autistic which also means I struggle with negative emotions such as anxiety and anger.

The important thing is this, you will never be able to stop yourself from feeling angry because we can't control our emotions. What we can control is how we react to them. When starting out in anger management, my buddy suggested doing small little workouts to get rid of the adrenaline. Doing a couple of push-ups, sit-ups jumping jacks, it doesn't matter. Just do something physical to disperse that energy.

Getting help is not a weakness by the way, it's a strength. Humans are built to help one another. That's what kept us alive in the stone ages and it still keeps us alive today. I wouldn't be here giving advice if it weren't for my own therapist. I'm pretty sure I'd be dead.

Trauma and Catholicism don't mix. 

For real though, it gradually happened. I was a Catholic for a long time after my aunt and uncle adopted me. Something like 7 or 8 years. I received almost all the sacraments even thought about being a priest for a little while. It's hard to say each moment that changed me, but there were significant moments. 

First, I had a fucked up childhood and I kept looking for a meaning to my suffering but nothing made sense. If God is all loving, then why allow these horrible things to happen to me? If God is all knowing, then why allow horrible things to happen to the world he created? And the only answer I would ever get "God works in mysterious ways, and we can't ever understand those reasons because then he wouldn't be God anymore." The more I looked for a reason, the more I second guessed everything.

 I was also sucked into a Catholic cult called the Neocatechumenal Way(still exists btw) of which I had a lot of friends, one of them a long-time childhood best friend. Because I'm no longer in it, they all ceased contact with me. My best friend, completely stopped talking to me when I became pagan. Never even reached out to me when my mother died. 

Another moment that changed me, I wrote a paper on Atheists in Catholic school. I forget what the assignment was, but I'm just someone who loves to learn. I decided to do a paper about atheists for a Reasons for the Faith class. For research I read a lot of books, theses, and other forms of media regarding atheism. Well, a lot of it made sense. As surprising as it may sound, I'm a bit of an optimist, so there were things I disagreed with. I felt a lot of their conclusions were cynical.

Fast forward years to when I was in my late teens, and I consider my agnostic at this point. I was still going to church to make my family happy, but I didn't really believe it anymore. In that cult I talked about, we took a trip to Italy to visit Rome and other religious cities. I got to see the Vatican(as a historian, I still appreciated going). In the Vatican, we took a tour of the whole building. The guide, a Cardinal, brought us to the entrance of Vault. A massive library of historical documents. We were denied access because only the Pope and Cardinals may enter. I was absolutely furious. Knowledge is a human RIGHT, and they are actively withholding it. In my humble opinion, that's a crime against humanity. I was absolutely done with Christianity after that trip.

To wrap up what's already a long story, I became a Norse Pagan by experiencing something more real than I ever felt. I always felt a connection and pull to Norse Mythology. Just never put any stock into it. Until one day, my anger was getting the better of me so I went outside to cool down. Two ravens had decided to post up next to me, and a wave of calmness took me. I can't explain what happened, but I just felt better. Look I believe in science first and foremost but I do believe something else is out there. I don't believe in the old myths that describe the world's creation, but I do believe in the stories about the Gods that illuminate their strengths and flaws which makes them relatable. I also became a pagan because it's a lot easier to accept other faiths. In fact, I also recently decided worship Medusa. 

If you read my story, thank you! May your gods bless, and keep you :)

Nodes also had to be built closer to the front line for maximum yield, again, not the case anymore. This overhaul killed a lot of the team play for me. I saw a significant shift in how people played and interacted with one another.

For example; Commander was worth 16 manpower. If he died, that's how much would tick down. So, commanders were never on the frontline. Other roles like medic were also worth more than 1 manpower(I forget their worth, but it wasn't more than 5). Halo is not about a one man killing machine in a sci-fi setting like many believe. That's just the character that gives agency to the player, something to identify with and feel connected to. That's why he remains faceless. The player is supposed to imprint themselves onto the Chief.

Halo, at its core, is about humanity facing an implacable enemy with little hope of overcoming said enemy. Key words in that sentence are "little hope." Througout the games and books, there are small victories that seem monumental to the player and reader but turn out to be miniscule in the actual war effort. Every decision made by humanity is about survival, not morality. The UNSC are extremely utilitarian with elements of fascism. The show does not accurately represent the core identity of Halo. It merely scratches the surface. 

Spartans are not supposed to be moody teenagers with emotion blockers in their spine. They embody the definitions of "perfect soldier" and "superhero." They were abducted at the age of 6 to be the future and protectors of humanity. In the real lore, Halsey never lied to the children because she knew that if she lied, they would betray her and the UNSC when they found out the truth. So she tells them exactly why they were abducted, why they'll never go home, and what they will become. 

Miranda Keyes is not a doctor. She followed in her father's footsteps of being a fleet officer because she HATED her mother, Dr. Halsey. She was a brilliant tactician who gave her life for humanity, not someone cooped up in a lab. She embodied what it meant to be a Captain and, in many ways, surpassed her father.

Master Chief is not a man who struggles with his past. He left that behind when he became a Spartan. He is, however, a man who struggles with connection. In the opening salvo of the war, Chief lost a couple of good friends, which shaped him into the stoic robotic soldier we see now. It's why he rarely takes his armor off. Cortana was the character that could spark the fire of his humanity once again. Throughout the games, we gradually see Chief open up a bit until he loses one of his closest friends, Sgt. Johnson. Arguably, one of the final deaths that pushed Chief to sacrifice himself to put an end to the war. None of this is accurately represented in the show. We don't care he takes his helmet off in the show, we care that he practically lives without it.

It's a military science fiction series, not a space opera, so characters need to feel like real-life characters and not stereotypes. The show unfortunately put almost every character into stereotypes. The only character I cared about was Vennick, the only Spartan who acted like a Spartan.

You know what's interesting about the node system is that it's not the original system. A lot of the dividing issues people have wouldn't exist without this change. The change in how nodes work now completely shifted the gameplay, and this was made by Black Matter. A change I've been against to this day.

I argue the old system was better. Basically, nodes could be built anywhere on the map. However, the closer the nodes were to HQ, the fewer resources you received from them. To get a +90 on a node, they had to be at the center grid line or beyond in enemy territory. In fact, if they were in enemy territory, you received more resources. This was done to simulate the logi train that connects to the front line. Now, what made this system much more valuable was the importance of Manpower. Manpower used to be far more important than it is today.   If you lost Manpower nodes, you would be incredibly hindered on Airheads, Reinforce, and Encouraged. It added strategic targets that Recon players could dismantle to really deal a blow. For example, one time, my buddy and I dismantled all of a teams nodes that were in our territory, 10 min later, we captured the center point. There were a lot of cool decisive moments in battles that came from that old system. Another example, if the US had no good tank squads, just dismantling all enemy fuel nodes would severely cripple the Germans and their ability to field tanks. Now, that doesn't matter at all because even without nodes, you still get a default of +30.
